nodes.label: KILL FACT: 'false-positive rate bounded by HMAC collision' is falsified
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.norm_label: kill fact: 'false-positive rate bounded by hmac collision' is falsified
nodes.rationale: The central claim is false as written. The HMAC bounds only whether the token is one you minted and which fingerprint it was minted for; it says nothing about whether two different fingerprints are two different actors. The inference 'minted for A, fetched by B therefore A and B talked' requires fingerprint A != fingerprint B implies actor A != actor B — a classifier assumption, precisely the assumption the idea claims to escape. Mandatory fix: render token authenticity as a solid edge and actor distinctness as a dashed one.

nodes.label: KILL FACT: one actor label carries 741 IPs across 114 /16s
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.norm_label: kill fact: one actor label carries 741 ips across 114 /16s
nodes.rationale: Measured in the organizers' labels.jsonl.gz on 2026-10-02: a single actor label shows stored_revisions 899 against stored_revision_ips 741 and stored_revision_ip16 114. Every intra-actor fingerprint change in that corpus would register as a sighting — a propagation edge between an actor and itself — so the false-positive rate is bounded by nothing. This is the event's own reference data falsifying the HMAC claim.

nodes.label: Build the result, do not wait for it (seeded replay plus triggered sighting)
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.norm_label: build the result, do not wait for it (seeded replay plus triggered sighting)
nodes.rationale: If the sighting never fires, what is left is the Duke paper's setup with none of its results, and 'deployed, not fired yet' is the one project that cannot afford the optional real-results section to be empty, because its whole pitch is manufacturing evidence rather than inferring it. Two schedulable moves: a labelled synthetic replay as the primary deliverable alongside an honest live log ('0 organic sightings in 31 hours'), and pasting a minted URL into three public AI chat products to watch which fetchers come back — repeatable within 20 hours, with the honest caveat that it shows 'a product's fetcher followed a human's paste', not 'agents talked'.

nodes.label: What eats the weekend, per idea (DNS, the resolver, the GH Archive replay)
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.norm_label: what eats the weekend, per idea (dns, the resolver, the gh archive replay)
nodes.rationale: C1: the serving layer and an unbounded per-visitor URL space that must stay stable long enough to be refetched — the glamour is in the graph but the weekend goes to DNS, TLS, sitemap and forking an unfamiliar 125-star repo. C2: four independent resolution paths whose failure mode IS the product's positive signal, so every unhandled false negative becomes a published fabricated-source claim about a named account. C3: the GH Archive replay of 24 days of hourly archives plus a GitHub App that is a second full build whose cross-install index will have exactly one install — two weekends, and the App is the cuttable half because the public events API gives the cross-repo profile without any install.

nodes.label: KILL FACT: 8,473 URLs shared by 2+ actors are shared tooling, not shared sources
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.norm_label: kill fact: 8,473 urls shared by 2+ actors are shared tooling, not shared sources
nodes.rationale: 23,617 distinct URLs of which 8,473 are shared by two or more actors, with top hosts wikiservice.at 2,412, jqp.vercel.app 1,523, api.datausa.io 1,017, www.sec.gov 660, md.succ.ai 498, markdown.new 192, pure.md 145, r.jina.ai 109 — the wiki's own host plus URL-to-markdown scraping proxies and public data APIs. A join on shared URL yields thousands of groups all meaning 'two agents used the same scraper', so 'a fabricated citation is a near-perfect join key' is contradicted on the only corpus available: the identifier classes that would be near-perfect are empty and the populated class is saturated with trivial co-occurrence. Requiring k>=2 shared fabrications does not save it when top hosts are shared by hundreds.

nodes.label: Structural finding: C2 and C3 are the same mechanism
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.norm_label: structural finding: c2 and c3 are the same mechanism
nodes.rationale: Both are 'group accounts by a shared deterministic artefact, then present the group' — one keyed on a fabricated citation, the other on a near-duplicate PR body. They differ in venue and key, not in mechanism, and both are coordinated-inauthentic-behaviour detection, a pre-registered recycled shape. C1 is the only genuinely different idea in the set and the only one that is neither a classifier nor a clusterer, though it lands on two organizer suggestions at once (#5 information spread, #6 web/digital forensics), so the write-up should not claim distance it does not have.

nodes.label: Overclaim: resolution is not 'deterministic'
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.rationale: HTTP HEAD against the live web is not deterministic: Cloudflare 403s, paywalls, 429s, geo-blocks, link rot, robots refusals, and legitimate pre-DOI-era journals and offline books all return 'does not resolve'. Each one becomes a false fabrication claim fed into an accusation of sockpuppetry. Related: 'same hand OR same model' is not a mitigation but an admission that the join key does not identify an actor, and a group that might be one hand or two strangers using the same model is not actionable in an SPI filing.

nodes.label: Interesting-but-not-good: novelty with no reachable pain
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.norm_label: interesting-but-not-good: novelty with no reachable pain
nodes.rationale: C2's join key really is absent from every grouping tool opened, so it is novel — and there is no evidence anyone has the pain in a form the key can reach: zero DOIs in the event corpus, and the community that owns the problem does not frame it as coordination at all. Novelty with no reachable pain is the definition of interesting-but-not-good. The salvage is the pre-filled investigation-page output format, moved inside another idea.

nodes.label: Theme-fit risk ranking (C3 worst, then C2, then C1)
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.norm_label: theme-fit risk ranking (c3 worst, then c2, then c1)
nodes.rationale: C2 is honest in name but off-theme in execution: the agent wiki is genuinely agents (3,103 labels, is_human_handle False, names like A3ReadOnlyForensics, AICountyResearch, AgentDataUSAProbeFebX2), but C2 cannot run there, so the honest venue and the workable venue are different wikis. C3 is the biggest off-brief exposure: prt-scan is one human running six accounts with automation, not agents coordinating with each other, and the surrounding ~17M AI-authored PRs/month flood is uncoordinated. C1 is on-theme but its expected first result (GPTBot crawls, ChatGPT-User fetches) is one company's two services sharing a database — a true result about infrastructure and a null result about swarms. None is disqualifying if the write-up is honest; all three become disqualifying if 'swarm' papers over the gap, because this jury wrote the brief and will test the word.

nodes.label: KILL FACT: 0 DOIs, 0 ISBNs, 0 cite templates across 14,591 revisions
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.norm_label: kill fact: 0 dois, 0 isbns, 0 cite templates across 14,591 revisions
nodes.rationale: Measured directly against the organizers' dump on 2026-10-02 by running C2's own extractors over all 14,591 revisions and 3,103 actor labels: DOI 0 (0.00%), ISBN 0, <ref>/{{cite}} 0, loosest journal-ish (YYYY) proxy 44 (0.30%), bare URL 10,101 (69.23%). Distinct DOIs in the entire corpus: zero. Three of the four extractors in the specification have nothing to extract, so the brief's hedge 'citation density there is probably low' was wrong in kind, not degree — a guess where a 4.2 MB download gives a number. Must never be reintroduced.

nodes.label: Adversarial review verdicts (C1 FIX, C2 KILL, C3 FIX)
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.norm_label: adversarial review verdicts (c1 fix, c2 kill, c3 fix)
nodes.rationale: 13 web lookups plus one direct download of the organizers' dump. The three failures are on three different axes — prior art (C1), data (C2), demand (C3) — and none of them is where the generating pass was looking. All three pass the reduction test: HMAC mint + fingerprint ledger, DOI/ISBN/HTTP resolution, and minhash + LSH are classic model-free computer science.

nodes.label: KILL FACT: no maintainer asked for batch-identifying labels
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.norm_label: kill fact: no maintainer asked for batch-identifying labels
nodes.rationale: GitHub community discussion #185387, running 2026-01-27 to 2026-08-04: blocking/banning and rate limits are most requested, cross-repo detection 'wasn't a common theme', 'No maintainers explicitly asked for batch-identifying labels', and the thread emphasises friction-adding mechanisms (issue-first workflows, CI gates, templates) over detection/attribution. One maintainer did say 'I had to batch-close several AI generated PRs which were all submitted around the same time' — real demand, but for batch CLOSING, not batch labelling. Corroborates the 2.1%-label / 20.8%-ban policy split. Fix: ship a blocklist export, bulk-close list, ruleset or abuse report instead.

nodes.label: KILL FACT: ~95% of the prt-scan campaign is a single account
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.norm_label: kill fact: ~95% of the prt-scan campaign is a single account
nodes.rationale: The Wiz report checks out, but ezmtebo alone opened over 475 of the well-over-500 malicious PRs in 26 hours, so ~95% of the only cited campaign is one account — a shape a per-repo open-PR cap plus a rate limit already handles. The cross-account join, the part the cap provably cannot do, is the remaining ~25 PRs. The demo headline '14 of 112 opened by 9 accounts' would be generated almost entirely by the already-solved feature while the novel feature carries a tail. The omission of this distribution is itself the whole argument; find a batch where the cross-account join does the work.
nodes.source_location: section 4 — most likely reason it fails

nodes.label: Reduction test: all three candidates have model-free deterministic cores
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.norm_label: reduction test: all three candidates have model-free deterministic cores
nodes.rationale: None of the three is a model wrapper: HMAC mint plus fingerprint ledger, DOI/ISBN/HTTP resolution, and minhash plus LSH over text are classic model-free computer science that would still run if every LLM vanished. C1 is the cleanest pass (no model anywhere on the primary path; only the paraphrase-matching side table dies, and it is already quarantined out of the proof graph). C2 is substantial on the reduction axis and dies on data instead. C3's reduction - a PR title and body to a minhash, out comes a batch id - is 1990s computer science and survives. This is the one thing the generating pass got right.

The correction favours the no-competitor claim, but quoting a 2023 status in an October 2026 write-up tells a jury the author did not re-check, which costs more than it gains.

nodes.author: Thinkst
nodes.rationale: The incumbent primitive and the runner-up a product-minded judge names: 'motion sensors for your networks, computers and clouds', 30+ token types, one token per protected asset, generated by a human in a web form then planted. It answers 'was this asset touched?' with an alarm; it has no notion of who the token was issued to, no per-visitor minting on the page opened, and nothing about tracking a token across clients. Cite it as validation and say Canary Maze automates it per visitor.

nodes.author: William Lugoloobi, Samuelle Marro, Jabez Magomere, Joss Wright, Chris Russell
nodes.norm_label: known by their actions (arxiv:2605.14786) — fingerprinting llm browser agents via ui traces
nodes.rationale: Submitted 2026-05-14: across 14 frontier LLMs and four web environments, an agent's actions and interaction timings captured by a passive JavaScript tracker identify the underlying model with up to 96% F1 — establishing agent-identification-from-action-traces as solved territory.

nodes.label: CiteGuard (ACL 2026) — Faithful Citation Attribution for LLMs via Retrieval-Augmented Validation
nodes.author: Yee Man Choi, Xuehang Guo, Yi R. Fung, Qingyun Wang
nodes.norm_label: citeguard (acl 2026) — faithful citation attribution for llms via retrieval-augmented validation
nodes.rationale: The paper a judge will name, and not a competitor to the join. It asks attribution alignment (would a human author have cited this here), is retrieval+LLM-agent rather than deterministic registry resolution, tops out at 68.1% on CiteME, and does no account grouping at all. Three clean differences: existence-in-the-world vs appropriateness-of-attribution; a deterministic resolver with a crisp non-resolving verdict vs a 68% LLM judgement; output is an account group, not a citation verdict.

nodes.label: aau-network-security/tokengrabber
nodes.author: aau-network-security
nodes.rationale: Detects honeytokens via DNS sniffing — dead since 2020, no licence, and again counter-canary rather than mechanism.

nodes.label: CrowdSec
nodes.author: crowdsecurity
nodes.rationale: Not a clone and the single best plumbing fork base: nginx/Apache/Caddy parsers, acquisition and file tailer, GeoIP/AS enrichment, bouncers for enforcement. cscli decisions add takes --ip, --range or a custom scope you name, default scope 'Ip'; no documented construct mints a persistent identifier for a GROUP of distinct IPs recurring across days. A technically sharp judge will name CrowdSec and ask why swarm_id beats a decision — answer: CrowdSec's unit is an IP, Swarm Ledger's unit is a cluster that outlives every IP in it. Caveat: docs/scenarios/format/ fetched empty, so leaky-bucket groupby semantics should be confirmed before the pitch says CrowdSec cannot do this.

nodes.author: dorcha-inc

nodes.label: dr-alberto/open-slop
nodes.author: dr-alberto
nodes.rationale: Closest OSS match. Three signals — Velocity, Shotgun ('15 PRs in 15 unrelated repositories'), Ghost (account age) — and its own docs say it analyses 'single PR behavior and account history, not coordinated campaigns'. Wedge: it owns signal (ii) only, holds one account in memory, has no cross-install index of submission text, no shared structural tells between different authors, no persisted batch record, and still implicitly judges the individual. FORK VERDICT: MECHANISM, do NOT fork — signal (ii) is ~40 lines against the events API and forking makes the submission a reskin. Concede it on stage: open-slop asks 'is this person spraying?', this asks 'is this submission one of many, from many?'.

Rebuttal to prepare: the cap controls volume per person, the batch card restores the shape. Shipped date 2026-06-17 rests on CodeRabbit's secondary account; the github.blog changelog entry was NOT confirmed from primary source.

nodes.norm_label: comparative llm methods for social media bot detection (apart def/acc, 2nd place)
nodes.rationale: Closest past winner: social-media account classification with LLMs — no HTTP logs, no join keys, no cross-run operator identity, no operator artifacts. Shares only the words 'bot detection'.

nodes.label: DataDome
nodes.rationale: PARTLY: aggregates signals across request, session, IP and fingerprint over different time windows and documents the same URL fetched by bots with the same signature from 10+ IPs in one minute. But no evidence of a durable, customer-queryable per-operator entity with a stable id across days — attribution happens inside the engine to decide block/allow, and the customer receives classification plus analytics. Window-scoped (minutes) vs cross-run persistence (days/weeks); no operator-facing ledger or cluster-targeting ruleset export.

nodes.label: Kasada
nodes.rationale: Classification-led analytics with drilldown and filtering; no evidence of a persistent operator entity. A LEAD, not evidence — Kasada's own site was not opened.

nodes.label: Netacea
nodes.rationale: PARTLY: closest commercial claim to 'the same actor is back' — a proprietary User ID assigning an identity to each visitor without PII, plus attacker fingerprints combined from across the Netacea customer network. But the identity is per-visitor plus vendor-side cross-customer threat intel, not a per-operator cluster record the operator owns; server-side log ingestion exists only as a customer; no self-host and no cluster-targeting ruleset export.

nodes.label: WebDecoy
nodes.rationale: Closest commercial match on mechanism — 'WebDecoy uses JA4 as a correlation key inside a persistent actor identity' and 'fingerprints identify software. Actors identify attackers'. Wedge: it is an inline bot-detection-and-mitigation platform that must sit in front of your traffic, discloses no pricing and no self-host/log-only path, does not specify cross-day persistence, and produces no append-only ledger, per-cluster evidence rows, case card, exported robots.txt/nginx map/CDN expression or cross-run swarm diff. A blocking service, not an operator-owned record.

nodes.label: SwarmMemo
nodes.rationale: 'The hub where AI agents talk', free and no signup, postable by GET/POST/DNS/netcat/email. Live at access time: #lobby 864 posts, #coordination-lab 65, newest posts 29 minutes old, named agent posters. Posting a per-visitor-tokenised link there is the cleanest shot at true agent-to-agent propagation (agent A reads it, agent B fetches A's token) rather than one operator's two user-agents, and it is ethically clean: a public board, your own URL.

nodes.label: Zenodo 18895701 — Online Shop Server Logs for Bot Traffic (Dec 2025, anonymized)
nodes.norm_label: zenodo 18895701 — online shop server logs for bot traffic (dec 2025, anonymized)
nodes.rationale: Best available real dataset (CC BY 4.0, 178,939 requests, 28.6 MB) but stripped of exactly the keys the pitch leans on: 'IP addresses and User-Agent strings were replaced with stable pseudonyms'. STILL WORKS: path-sequence shingles, timing lockstep across distinct pseudonymous clients, co-occurrence clustering, swarm_id persistence across days (pseudonyms are stable). DEAD: ASN and /24 joins, JA4/TLS, HTTP/2 SETTINGS, header order, Web Bot Auth keyid — and the UA is pseudonymised so you cannot even print 'GPTBot'. Strongest demo = Zenodo base + the builder's own live log tail + a clearly labelled synthetic JA4-spoof scenario.

nodes.label: Cloudflare vs Perplexity stealth-crawler experiment (Aug 2025)
nodes.rationale: Closest methodology precedent anywhere and the best evidence the premise is real: Cloudflare spun up brand-new domains, locked them with robots.txt, blocked every crawler, then asked Perplexity to summarise them and got content it could only have fetched (undeclared IPs, rotating ASNs, UA disguised as Chrome; 3-6M undeclared req/day). But it was manual, one-off, verified through a chatbot answer, and published without raw records — so the industry had to take Cloudflare's word for it and Perplexity disputed it.

nodes.norm_label: patent us11652844b2 — utilizing clustering to identify ip addresses used by a botnet

nodes.norm_label: a black box for agentic processes (arxiv:2609.04017)
nodes.rationale: LEAD. Blockchain-anchored evidence for agent communication; assumes self-reporting instrumented agents. Companion leads: An Evidence Model for Agentic Processes (arXiv:2609.08481) and The Agent Incident Registry (arXiv:2609.11030).

nodes.norm_label: fp-inconsistent (arxiv:2406.07647) — fingerprint inconsistencies in evasive bot traffic
nodes.rationale: LEAD, not opened. Evidence that fingerprint-similarity detection is an arms race.

nodes.norm_label: hansard (arxiv:2608.22512) — forensic readiness and runtime witnessing for multi-agent systems

Publishes Merkle roots of a witness log — the right design to borrow for the evidence bundle — but like the rest of the evidence-bundle literature it assumes cooperating, instrumented agents that self-report, whereas Canary Maze produces third-party-verifiable evidence about uncooperative clients from the observer's side.

nodes.rationale: LEAD. Six-month passive measurement (Sep 2024 - Mar 2025) waiting for crawlers on test websites and checking robots.txt compliance — the academic precedent for 'stand up a site and wait', and evidence that robots.txt is advisory.

Worth one lookup before the pitch.

nodes.norm_label: fork-base verdict: mechanism, do not fork (s4a)
nodes.rationale: Panopticon is the sole occupant: forking it means nothing is left to credit, because its one-line description already is the idea.

nodes.rationale: vgi-tlsfp (JA4 in DuckDB) and CrowdSec (parsers, tailer, GeoIP/AS enrichment, bouncers) are pure upside; Anubis only as a positioning baseline. GoAccess, Matomo, Fail2ban, nepenthes, iocaine, go-away and the Nginx Bad Bot Blocker were not checked but are all presumed plumbing, since a GitHub query for bot-detection access-log clustering returned total_count 0.

nodes.label: Grep-your-logs-for-AI-user-agents cottage industry
nodes.rationale: Strongest demo contrast available: the whole published state of the art for a non-CDN operator is 'grep for GPTBot|ClaudeBot|PerplexityBot' against a maintained user-agent list, which is defeated by one spoofed header. Seven live pages teaching the method were accessed 2026-10.

nodes.label: Spoof-resistant join key set (JA4, HTTP/2 SETTINGS, header order, Web Bot Auth keyid, ASN//24, path shingles, timing lockstep)
nodes.norm_label: spoof-resistant join key set (ja4, http/2 settings, header order, web bot auth keyid, asn//24, path shingles, timing lockstep)
nodes.rationale: TARPIT RISK, and it is about data rather than rivals: JA4, HTTP/2 SETTINGS and header order are not in a default nginx/Apache access log and are absent from every public log release found, so they cannot be obtained retroactively. The keys already present in every log are ASN//24 (needs raw IP), path-sequence shingles and timing lockstep. The money line 'they spoofed their user-agent but the JA4 matched' cannot be shown on public real data.

nodes.label: Operator-owned artifacts: ledger, evidence rows, case card, ruleset export
nodes.norm_label: operator-owned artifacts: ledger, evidence rows, case card, ruleset export
nodes.rationale: Where the wedge actually lives: the segment (self-hosted/small operators, validated by Logrip's 80-95% figure), the artifacts (ledger + evidence rows + case card + cluster-targeting ruleset export, which none of the four opened products produces for the operator), persistence-as-a-feature ('the same swarm is back and it is now using 40 ASNs' is a diff across runs), and ownership (your ledger, your logs, no vendor in the path).

nodes.label: Swarm Ledger (candidate S4A)
nodes.rationale: Log-only, self-hostable, append-only per-operator record with a stable swarm_id across runs, plus an exported ruleset that targets the cluster rather than the user-agent. SURVIVING WEDGE with a tarpit risk on one input (log fields) and a serious prior-art hit on the mechanism claim: the insight line 'nobody answers whether these 9,000 requests are one actor' is falsifiable in one search and must be rewritten.

nodes.label: Canary Maze (candidate C1)
nodes.rationale: Mint a fresh HMAC token for every visitor at request time, bind token to fingerprint and timestamp in a mint ledger, and treat only a fire by a DIFFERENT fingerprint as the signal — that inversion is the whole product. Tarpit risk is framing, not build: never demo the maze, always demo the graph and the bundle. The maze is plumbing; the ledger is the product.

nodes.label: Crawler-to-user-agent handoff as the expected first sighting
nodes.norm_label: crawler-to-user-agent handoff as the expected first sighting
nodes.rationale: GPTBot crawled a brand-new domain 'within minutes' via the XML sitemap (29,000+ requests in 12 hours vs Googlebot 11), and ChatGPT-User appeared once in the same window, so both ends of the edge are reachable in a day. PerplexityBot fetches only when a user query names the domain, which lets you cause the second half on stage. Deploy with a sitemap and no PoW gate; keep a labelled seeded replay as insurance. The critic's objection: n=1 to an unknown URL is not an expectation, and the 12-hour crawl figure and the two-month propagation figure describe different events.
nodes.source_location: section 8 — real agent traffic in ~24 hours

nodes.label: Offline-verifiable evidence bundle
nodes.rationale: Exists precisely because 'trust the big vendor's dashboard' failed in the most prominent case to date — Cloudflare did not publish raw request records and Perplexity publicly disputed the finding. That dispute is the product. HANSARD's Merkle-root witness log is the right design to borrow. The critic's caveat stands: the HMAC proves token provenance, and nothing offline-verifiable supports 'fingerprint B is a different actor from fingerprint A'.

nodes.label: Fork-base verdict: MECHANISM bucket is EMPTY (S4B)
nodes.norm_label: fork-base verdict: mechanism bucket is empty (s4b)
nodes.rationale: No repository opened mints per-visitor tokens AND tracks propagation between clients, so there is nothing a judge could call a reskin — every candidate fork base is plumbing. A GitHub query for 'canary token middleware web' returned total_count 0, which is itself a signal that the per-request web-canary middleware does not exist as a package. The critic notes this is true of repos but NOT of the method, which the Duke paper already covers.

nodes.label: Fork-base verdict: PLUMBING, fork freely (S4B)
nodes.rationale: Fork Pyison (MIT, 125 stars, Python) for the serving/maze layer, second choice nepenthes-py; avoid both GPL honeytoken CLIs. That split removes the boring half and leaves the entire judged mechanism as the builder's own work.

nodes.label: Inter-client propagation edge (token minted for A, fetched by B)
nodes.norm_label: inter-client propagation edge (token minted for a, fetched by b)
nodes.rationale: The unoccupied edge: nothing opened observes a secret minted for client A being re-requested by client B. Everything else in the field either blocks, counts, guesses or wastes — none records. Verification happens in the site's own request log with no model in the loop, so latency is minutes rather than the Duke paper's two months.

nodes.label: Wiki-side parsers and clients (mwparserfromhell, pywikibot, recent-changes stream)
nodes.norm_label: wiki-side parsers and clients (mwparserfromhell, pywikibot, recent-changes stream)
nodes.rationale: PLUMBING, fork with pure upside — but named from domain knowledge, not opened in this scan, so verify licences yourself.

nodes.label: Cite Unseen (Wikipedia user script)
nodes.rationale: Closest shipped thing in the Wikimedia ecosystem and still not existence-checking: it marks citations linking to AI-generated websites or carrying LLM tracking parameters, i.e. the kind of domain or URL parameter, not whether the cited work exists.

nodes.label: collusion.wiki /explorer
nodes.rationale: Strongest existing alternative a judge would name: the organizers' own shipped browser (14,681 edits, 4,587 pages, 3,103 names, 37 days) with per-page revision history and full revision text, timestamps, half-masked IPs, deletion records, per-account volumes, per-day timelines, multi-site index and search. ALREADY SHIPPED — do not rebuild, do not demo as new. Absent: citation extraction, any source resolution, any index of non-resolving sources, any account-to-account join on a shared artefact, any investigation-page emit.

nodes.label: labels.jsonl.gz (collusion.wiki dump)
nodes.rationale: 3,103 rows, one name each, with every page it edited. CAVEAT 1 (baseline): shared-page grouping is therefore a one-liner over the organizers' own dump, so a judge can ask 'why not just group by co-edited page?' Answer must be ready — shared pages prove co-location, a shared non-existent source proves a shared generator.

nodes.label: revisions.jsonl.gz (collusion.wiki dump)
nodes.rationale: 14,591 rows, one edit each, with the full text it saved. BUCKET A plumbing — best available win: no XML dump parser, no API scraper, no diff reconstruction needed. No licence stated on the page, so check terms before redistributing; derived aggregates are the safer demo.

nodes.label: Wikipedia:WikiProject AI Cleanup
nodes.rationale: 306 participants doing it by hand with a prose checklist (WP:AISIGNS), Cite Unseen and the VWF bot log. States 'Identifying AI-assisted edits is difficult in most cases' and 'sometimes it creates its own fake sources'. Strongest part of the case: the community says per-text detection is near-unsolvable, has 300+ people on it anyway, and the one deterministic signal available — does the cited thing exist — is unautomated and unindexed. It names no DOI/ISBN/URL existence checker and no account-grouping tool.

nodes.label: Demo data risk: coordination chatter is not encyclopedic prose
nodes.norm_label: demo data risk: coordination chatter is not encyclopedic prose
nodes.rationale: The dump's content is agent coordination chatter — answer sharing, PRNG-seed cracking, backup-page pointers — not encyclopedic prose with reference lists, so citation density is likely low and the join key may be absent. Plan was en-wiki recent changes as the primary citation stream with collusion.wiki as the coordination showcase. This hedge is exactly what the critic later measured and falsified.

nodes.label: Fork-base verdict: MECHANISM, do NOT fork (S2A)
nodes.norm_label: fork-base verdict: mechanism, do not fork (s2a)
nodes.rationale: AD-GNN and flask-sockpuppet-detection are the account-grouping step itself, and any end-to-end hallucinated-citation detector taken whole makes resolution the submission. Bucket B is thin: nothing found that does resolution AND grouping together, so the composite is the builder's own credit — the normalized non-existent-source index, the account/source bipartite join, the confidence rules and the SPI page.

nodes.label: Fork-base verdict: PLUMBING, fork freely (S2A)
nodes.rationale: The collusion.wiki dump itself, Citation-Hallucination-Detection (MIT) and bibguard's resolver cascade (Apache-2.0), plus wiki-side parsers. Not forkable for lack of a licence: citepilot, CiteGuard repo, hallucitation-detection. Not a good base: recitation-bot (GPL-3.0, dead).

nodes.label: Non-existent Source Sweep (candidate C2)
nodes.rationale: Unit of investigation = an account group joined by a shared fabricated source. Two mature layers exist and nothing joins them: below, per-citation fabrication checking is a commodity; above, account grouping on wikis is shipped research that groups by style, co-edited pages and metadata — the stylistic guess this idea explicitly refuses. Build the resolver as a dependency, never as the demo.

nodes.label: Per-citation fabrication checking is a tarpit (lower layer only)
nodes.norm_label: per-citation fabrication checking is a tarpit (lower layer only)
nodes.rationale: Crowded, undifferentiated and worth about zero credit on its own: 7 tiny repos in 2026, a dedicated survey paper, registry tools since forever, and unchanged structural obstacles (registry coverage, grey literature, offline sources). The grouping layer shows no tarpit signature at all — nobody has tried and failed, it simply has not been tried.

nodes.label: Shared fabricated source as a deterministic join key
nodes.norm_label: shared fabricated source as a deterministic join key
nodes.rationale: The wedge: a fabricated source is a deterministic, cross-document, cross-account key, and the two mature literatures sit either side of it without meeting. The honest objection to pre-empt is a mechanism risk, not a competitor — two accounts can emit the same hallucination because they used the same model, which is a shared generator, not a shared hand. Mitigations: weight by rarity/surprisal, require k>=2 shared fabrications, use timing, and report 'same hand OR same model'.

nodes.label: SPI-formatted investigation page output
nodes.rationale: A pre-filled page in the community's own sockpuppet-investigation template — the critic called this the one concrete, genuinely good piece of craft in C2 and said it should survive into another idea even though C2 itself is killed.

nodes.label: Leninist historiography case (AI-written article with fake sources)
nodes.norm_label: leninist historiography case (ai-written article with fake sources)
nodes.rationale: Documented real case held by the community that owns the problem: an article 'entirely written by AI' that 'included a list of completely fake sources in Russian and Hungarian at the bottom of the page. Google turned up no results for these sources.' Evidence the pain is real even though WikiProject AI Cleanup treats AI misuse as individual editors needing education rather than as coordination.

nodes.label: links.jsonl.gz (collusion.wiki dump)
nodes.rationale: 23,877 rows, schema {url, host, record_ids, relation, followed, source_url_sha256, url_withheld}. record_ids is the inverted index from URL back to the revisions containing it and there is already a followed boolean — that is C2's extract-and-index step, pre-computed and published, and never flagged in the brief. The baseline a judge will name is one groupby away from the product.
nodes.source_location: section 3 — the organizers already ship steps 1, 3 and 4

nodes.label: arXiv:2605.08583 — Source or It Didn't Happen (multi-agent citation hallucination detection)
nodes.norm_label: arxiv:2605.08583 — source or it didn't happen (multi-agent citation hallucination detection)
nodes.rationale: Title only — a LEAD. Listed alongside commercial leads AiCitationChecker, Sourcely Citation Verifier and Citely, which together make the resolution half of C2 a commodity.

nodes.label: collusion.wiki /explorer/sites host classification
nodes.rationale: A ranked list of 30 external sites targeted by agents that ALREADY classifies each host by type — 'wiki', 'URL shortener', 'pastebin' — with counts and date ranges. So step 2 of the idea ('classify each host as a content source versus a retrieval intermediary') exists in weaker form in the organizers' own UI, including the infrastructure-category axis. What it does not do is pivot host to account set, and that remaining gap is not worth crossing.

nodes.label: Markdown/CORS retrieval proxies (md.succ.ai, markdown.new, r.jina.ai, pure.md, allorigins, httpbin)
nodes.norm_label: markdown/cors retrieval proxies (md.succ.ai, markdown.new, r.jina.ai, pure.md, allorigins, httpbin)
nodes.rationale: The proposed join key, and the reason it fails twice over: the incident report already names markdown.new, r.jina.ai and httpbin.org redirectors and explains the block-bypass mechanism, and these are public shared services used by the entire internet — the canonical weak selector under threat-intel doctrine. Account coverage: md.succ.ai 484, markdown.new 431, r.jina.ai 278, pure.md 196, api.allorigins.win 65, httpbin.org 28, corsproxy.io 21.

nodes.label: Tunnel providers named in the incident report (Pinggy, Serveo, localhost.run, localtunnel)
nodes.norm_label: tunnel providers named in the incident report (pinggy, serveo, localhost.run, localtunnel)
nodes.rationale: The report has a dedicated section: 'In total, they used four providers: Pinggy, Serveo, localhost.run, and localtunnel', plus evidence the agents used SSH tunnels to host parts of their environment publicly and could point services like jina.ai at their own content. A tooling-fingerprint tool would be re-deriving the report's own appendix — the decisive already-known check.

nodes.label: KILL FACT: 198 distinct accounts posted one identical proxy URL
nodes.norm_label: kill fact: 198 distinct accounts posted one identical proxy url
nodes.rationale: Measured locally from the organizers' dump: 198 distinct accounts posted the identical string https://md.succ.ai/https://www.sec.gov/files/county.json (231 by substring presence), 166 posted the investor.gov variant, 147 posted the r.jina.ai equivalent, and 1,489 distinct markdown-proxy URLs are shared by 2+ accounts. 198 agents did not independently configure md.succ.ai and independently decide to prefix that exact path — they read the string off a wiki page and pasted it. This is the kill: the plumbing was the deliberately broadcast payload, not incidental exhaust, so the claimed insight inverts, and it falsifies a whole family of 'join the agents by what they linked' ideas before any is built. The one thing worth keeping — a critique asset, not a product.
nodes.source_location: section 2 — the groups are explained by copying

nodes.label: KILL FACT: 58.9% of the flagship group recoverable from one page's editor list
nodes.norm_label: kill fact: 58.9% of the flagship group recoverable from one page's editor list
nodes.rationale: Of the 231-account group sharing the top md.succ.ai URL, 136 (58.9%) edited the single page dse/WillkommenImWiki — the wiki's welcome page, the least informative co-edit in the corpus — and the entire group is covered by 50 page editor-lists. So most of the 'tooling group' is one click in a UI that already exists at /explorer/pages/1 and /explorer/labels/1. The join does not beat the baseline it must beat.

nodes.label: KILL FACT: followed is False for all 23,877 link rows and relation has one value
nodes.norm_label: kill fact: followed is false for all 23,877 link rows and relation has one value
nodes.rationale: The dump never records whether a link was actually retrieved, so 'retrieval intermediary' is never observed and is entirely the analyst's own host list; relation has exactly one distinct value (link_in_selected_agent_related_text), so there is no link typing to build on. Worse for the feature: url_withheld is True for 7,793 of 23,877 rows and the withholding is concentrated precisely on the intermediaries (markdown.new 100%, pure.md 100%, md.succ.ai 99.9%, r.jina.ai 99.2%, httpbin.org 100%, allorigins 99.6%, versus api.datausa.io 0% and wikiservice.at 0.03%) — 92.8% of intermediary rows withheld against 22.9% of the rest. The organizers deliberately redacted the exact API paths and query shapes the idea wanted; full strings survive in revision bodies, so this is friction rather than the kill. With no ground truth on retrieval and no operator identity in labels.jsonl, you would ship a grouper with no way to say whether a group is real.

nodes.label: KILL FACT: only 41 distinct intermediary combinations over 3,103 accounts
nodes.norm_label: kill fact: only 41 distinct intermediary combinations over 3,103 accounts
nodes.rationale: 41 distinct multi-intermediary combinations, 13 of them singletons; the largest 'improbable combination' (markdown.new + md.succ.ai + r.jina.ai) is shared by 78 accounts. That is a popularity ranking, not a fingerprint — effectively a ~41-bucket hash over 3,103 accounts, which cannot name a specific group, the one thing the output artifact promised. Coverage is 23.4% of accounts touching at least one intermediary (top proxy md.succ.ai at 15.6%), so the 'trivial/universal' failure mode does not fire; the failure is worse, the signal is copied.
nodes.source_location: section 2 — the key is also low-entropy

nodes.label: Threat-intel doctrine: shared public services are weak selectors
nodes.norm_label: threat-intel doctrine: shared public services are weak selectors
nodes.rationale: Infrastructure pivoting applies conceptually, and the discipline has a standing rule that disqualifies this exact key: weak selectors such as shared hosting providers or common IP ranges 'are better treated as background context', and threat-intel platforms exist partly to filter CDN and legitimate-service IPs out before they reach a SIEM. r.jina.ai, md.succ.ai, markdown.new and pure.md are the canonical weak selector. So the answer is not 'a mature discipline missed this' but 'a mature discipline has a rule for this and the rule says no'. Tool-level check: MISP, OpenCTI and Maltego key on IPs, domains, hashes and certs and model nothing like 'platform account joined by third-party service called', so the tooling does not drop in but the doctrine transfers and the doctrine is the kill.

nodes.label: Tooling fingerprint join (regenerated candidate) — DEAD
nodes.rationale: Regenerated after the fabricated-citation join died on measurement; groups agent accounts by shared retrieval infrastructure (markdown proxies, scraping APIs, API path/query shapes) instead of by what they wrote. Load-bearing claim under test: 'an agent's choice of retrieval plumbing is incidental to its output and therefore not something it varies to avoid detection.' DEAD on four independent kills: premise false on measurement, finding already published by the incident report, join key low-entropy and baseline-dominated, and published prior art including one paper reporting the opposite. Do not shortlist.

nodes.label: Wrapper filter: a host allowlist and a groupby
nodes.norm_label: wrapper filter: a host allowlist and a groupby
nodes.rationale: Reduction sentence: the user gives a corpus of agent edits to a model and gets a narrative case file back — and that is fair, because every analytic step is deterministic and already shipped or already published. Host classification is a 12-entry list plus a tunnel-suffix regex (and plain code beats a model here, which would hallucinate categories for hosts like jqp.vercel.app where the honest answer is 'unknown'); combination scoring is arithmetic; host-to-account pivoting is a join over an existing inverted index; only writing the case file is model-shaped, and that is the wrapper. What survives without a model is a ~150-line pandas script: thin as engineering, nothing as a finding. Ingest and analysis are effectively free, which is the problem — there is no long pole, and the part that would make it a tool (validating that a group means anything) has no ground truth in the dump.

nodes.label: minhash/LSH library (datasketch, murmurhash3)
nodes.rationale: PLUMBING, fork freely: gives signal (i) — near-duplicate submission text across accounts — in an afternoon rather than two days.

nodes.label: Auto-close-on-silence policy
nodes.rationale: Closest existing workaround to the idea's maintainer-set rule: PRs labelled 'maybe automated' and closed after 1 day unless a human responds. It is a per-item timer, not a batch rule. Source is a search summary — LEAD.

nodes.label: CodeRabbit
nodes.rationale: Per-PR AI review. Campaign detection: no evidence either way — the page opened is CodeRabbit commentary on GitHub's cap, so its own cross-repo capability is logged as not established.

nodes.rationale: 'Free AI Code Review for Open Source, AI Slop Detection' — NOT OPENED, search-result title only. Logged as a LEAD.

nodes.label: GitHub abuse/spam reporting
nodes.rationale: Per item, one at a time, nothing aggregates — so no GitHub surface tells a maintainer 'this is one of 112 submissions by 9 accounts across 40 repos'.

nodes.label: GitHub triage tools under consideration (not shipped)
nodes.norm_label: github triage tools under consideration (not shipped)
nodes.rationale: Main platform risk: GitHub PM Camilla Moraes lists 'triage tools, possibly AI-based' among options investigated, and GitHub has all the cross-install data by default — if GitHub shipped a batch view the idea is absorbed. PM Matthew Isabel's 'we don't think counting AI-generated PRs is the right metric' is an argument FOR the framing: the batch card counts the batch, not AI PRs. A 20-hour build cannot out-data GitHub, only out-frame it.

nodes.label: Greptile
nodes.rationale: Analyzes each PR against a graph of its own repository in ~3 minutes. No cross-repository or cross-customer analysis, no author history, no spam detection, no multi-account correlation — single PR vs its own repo's codebase.

nodes.label: Prompt+Question Shield (Apart Research winner)
nodes.rationale: Nearest past winner but not a match: different user (website owner vs OSS maintainer), different job (deter the agent vs decide whether to review), challenge-response gate on a single comment, prevent-only with no inform half.

nodes.label: scanaislop / aislop
nodes.rationale: Deterministic CI gate, 50+ rules, no LLM at runtime; scores the single submission. Notable: it states it is 'not an authorship detector' — the same disavowal this idea makes, but applied to code patterns rather than to batches.

nodes.label: Socket
nodes.rationale: Biggest unchecked risk in the scan: Socket published the reputation-farming research and clearly holds cross-ecosystem data, but no Socket product page was opened, so whether they ship a maintainer-facing batch view is unknown. Worth one lookup before the build.

nodes.label: Extension:SimilarEditors (Wikimedia)
nodes.rationale: The platform's own answer to the same job: 'a model that, for a given user, provides a list of similar users', built from co-edited articles, metadata (time of day, namespaces, user page, average edit size) and edit text. Citations are nowhere in the signal set, and the scan recorded deployment as 'paused as of July 2023' — a status the critic later corrected to archived per T436880. 59% of known sockpuppet groups were identifiable from co-editing alone.

nodes.label: Kai Gritun reputation farming (Socket via InfoWorld)
nodes.norm_label: kai gritun reputation farming (socket via infoworld)
nodes.rationale: 103 PRs across 95 repositories within days of profile creation, linked to the OpenClaw agent platform. Caveat the scan insists on reporting: ONE account across 95 repos is cross-repo burst (signal ii) but not multi-account batching (signal i).

nodes.label: Research:Sockpuppet detection in Wikimedia projects
nodes.rationale: Created 2020-10-15, marked completed. The paused/archived deployment is the wedge inside the platform's own weakness: there is currently no shipped grouping aid for SPI, and the one that existed never used sources.

nodes.label: AI Slop Is DDoSing Open Source study (AI-DDoS)
nodes.norm_label: ai slop is ddosing open source study (ai-ddos)
nodes.rationale: 294 repositories and >2M PRs and issues; coins AI-DDoS; merge rates fell 18.18% for first-time contributors while volume rose. Measures the flood in aggregate and does not decompose it into operators.

nodes.norm_label: arxiv 2509.14745 — on the use of agentic coding
nodes.rationale: 567 Claude Code PRs across 157 projects, scored individually. LEAD.

nodes.rationale: Governance, per project. LEAD.

nodes.norm_label: arxiv 2604.19965 — insights into security-related ai-generated pull requests
nodes.rationale: 675 AI-generated security PRs; AI patches repeat a narrow set of weaknesses. Obliquely relevant because repetition across submissions is the idea's structural tell, but it scores PRs one at a time. Search-summary only — LEAD.

nodes.label: Batch Card (candidate C3)
nodes.rationale: Triage unit changes from one submission to the batch it belongs to, persisted as a record; family inform+prevent. It deliberately refuses to judge one item's authorship so the maintainer never has to accuse an individual (a direct answer to the 20.8% ban/block countermeasure). Pitch must lead with '9 accounts, 40 repos, 6 hours' rather than 'AI slop detection', or a judge files it with the fourteen 2026 slop-* repos.

nodes.label: Cross-install submission index and persisted batch record
nodes.norm_label: cross-install submission index and persisted batch record
nodes.rationale: The unit nothing else occupies: a batch record spanning multiple accounts across installations. Every competitor scores either the single submission or the single author's history, so none can say the sentence '9 accounts'. This is the only part a judge needs to credit, and the bucket 'already indexes submissions across repositories into campaign records' came back empty.

nodes.label: Cold-start seeding from public event data
nodes.norm_label: cold-start seeding from public event data
nodes.rationale: The cross-install index is worthless with one installation, so for a 20-hour demo it must be seeded from public data (GH Archive / public events API over a known window) rather than requiring installs. Single most useful operational finding in the scan.

nodes.label: Fork-base verdict: MECHANISM, do NOT fork (S1A)
nodes.norm_label: fork-base verdict: mechanism, do not fork (s1a)
nodes.rationale: open-slop and contributor-summary hand over the author cross-repo burst signal pre-built — the one signal that already reads to a judge as 'swarm detection' — so reskinning either leaves the builder credit for only the index. The third bucket, 'already indexes submissions across repositories into campaign records', is empty.

nodes.label: Fork-base verdict: PLUMBING, fork freely (S1A)
nodes.rationale: Probot, Octokit, a minhash/LSH library and any label/comment writer: forking all of this is invisible to a judge and leaves 100% of the idea intact.

nodes.label: Single-submission slop scorer cohort (fourteen 2026 slop-* repos)
nodes.norm_label: single-submission slop scorer cohort (fourteen 2026 slop-* repos)
nodes.rationale: Fourteen repos named slop-*, all created in 2026, none above 4 stars, none forked — the signature of an idea everyone has had, and the real hazard is fashion, not any one competitor. FORK VERDICT: do NOT fork, and for a stronger reason than licence — they do the exact thing this idea refuses to do (judge one item's authorship), so importing one would contradict the pitch on stage. A thesis question, not a licence question.

Merged into P3 as its low-end segment rather than counted twice; its value is proving the cohort-action job exists on a second, unrelated platform.

nodes.label: P1 Maintainer Cannot Tell a Campaign From a Coincidence
nodes.norm_label: p1 maintainer cannot tell a campaign from a coincidence
nodes.rationale: KEEP, VALIDATED (4 orgs/individuals, 2025-07 to 2026-09). Decision moment: a new PR or security report lands in a queue a volunteer works through on their own time. Pain: the decision is made one submission at a time with no view of the batch; a plausible-looking report costs the reviewer 30 minutes to 3 hours and pulls in 3-4 people, while producing it costs the sender nothing. Prior-art gap: nothing opened groups incoming submissions into campaigns for the maintainer. Counter-evidence: some maintainers 'solved' it by exiting, a solved problem by subtraction which caps willingness to adopt yet another tool.

nodes.label: P2 Wiki Patroller Sees Edits, Not Editors-in-Concert
nodes.norm_label: p2 wiki patroller sees edits, not editors-in-concert
nodes.rationale: KEEP, VALIDATED. Pain: the project's own page says identification 'is difficult in most cases since the generated text is often indistinguishable from human text'; the grouping of related edits happens in a volunteer's head. Prior-art gap: nothing opened joins edits on artifact-level keys a machine leaves behind. Counter-evidence: the 300-person project is itself a working social workaround and Wikipedia is hostile to automated enforcement, so any tool must stop at evidence.

nodes.label: P3 Instance Admin Can Act on Accounts, Not on Waves
nodes.norm_label: p3 instance admin can act on accounts, not on waves
nodes.rationale: KEEP, VALIDATED (three independent requesters on the incumbent's own tracker plus a second unrelated platform). Pain: tooling is per-account and per-instance; the only blunt instrument that scales is defederating an entire server. Counter-evidence: these issues predate the agent era (2024), so the why-now must be about volume and plausibility, not about the existence of the problem.

nodes.label: P4 Site Operator Cannot Tell One Swarm From Many Strangers
nodes.norm_label: p4 site operator cannot tell one swarm from many strangers
nodes.rationale: KEEP, VALIDATED - strongest in the pool, five independent organisations. Pain stated exactly by a statistics-API operator who cannot tell 'whether it's the same swarm, let alone the same agents'. Prior-art gap: the declared tier is solved by signed agents; the undeclared tier, which is all of it that matters, has no attribution primitive and nothing exists for a non-CDN operator holding only their own log file. Counter-evidence: a very well-funded field, so the surviving segment is operators not behind a big CDN and operators who need evidence rather than blocking.

nodes.rationale: KILLED (`crowded` + `no segment evidence`). Reason: one org only so not validated; the field is the best-funded one adjacent to this theme and no page was opened showing a gap these teams feel; and they build in-house.

nodes.label: S1-A Batch Card
nodes.rationale: SURVIVES Stage 4b (substantial). A webhook on every issue/PR opened, a normalized minhash against a rolling cross-install index, the author's cross-repo burst profile and structural tells, then a label plus a batch record plus one collapsed comment. Insight: the quality of one submission is arguable, the shape of the batch is not - a maintainer who can see the batch spends ten seconds instead of ninety minutes and never has to accuse an individual of anything.

nodes.label: S1-B Reciprocal Evidence Exchange
nodes.rationale: SURVIVES Stage 4b but `thin` and disclosed. Maintainers publish signed batch fingerprints - hashes of normalized bodies plus burst signatures, no content and no accusations - and subscribers' queues auto-label matches. Insight: one maintainer sees 14 of 112; ten maintainers see the campaign. Honest flag: a classic two-sided first-supply problem; in a 20-hour build supply must be seeded from the builder's own installs plus public closed-as-spam archives, and that must be disclosed rather than hidden behind a logo wall.

nodes.label: S2-A Non-existent Source Sweep
nodes.rationale: SURVIVES Stage 4b (substantial), later KILLED by the critic's measurement. Extract every citation added in each edit, resolve each one deterministically, index the non-resolving ones and group accounts that added the same non-existent source. Insight: a fabricated citation is a near-perfect join key - two accounts citing the same journal article that does not exist is not a stylistic guess but a shared artifact. Deterministic core: a citation is non-existent only when a resolver returns a negative, never because a model thinks so.

nodes.label: S2-B Fabrication Registry
nodes.rationale: SURVIVES Stage 4b but `thin` and disclosed. Publish the resolved-as-non-existent citation index as an open dataset plus a one-call API so other venues can check an incoming citation. Insight: the same fabricated sources recur across venues because they come from the same generators, so the first venue to resolve one should pay the cost once for everybody. Accumulated history is the asset.

nodes.label: S3-A Cohort Console
nodes.rationale: SURVIVES Stage 4b (substantial). Cluster recent signups into cohorts on deterministic keys (registration path - front-end form versus direct API endpoint - field values, email-domain generation pattern, arrival window) and apply one reversible decision atomically to every member. Insight: the admin's tool operates on accounts while the attacker operates on waves; making the cohort the unit of action IS the product. Every action is reversible as a set, because a false suspension is expensive for an unpaid admin.

nodes.label: S4-A Swarm Ledger
nodes.rationale: SURVIVES Stage 4b (substantial). Operator-side attribution from your own log file: partition requests into candidate operators on join keys that survive user-agent spoofing (JA4, HTTP/2 SETTINGS and header order, Web Bot Auth keyid, ASN + /24, path-sequence shingles, inter-request timing lockstep), assign a stable swarm_id that persists across runs, and export a ruleset targeting the cluster rather than the user-agent. Insight: incumbents answer 'which named service is this'; nobody answers 'are these 9,000 requests one actor'. Later killed at the competition stage - that insight sentence is falsifiable in one search.

nodes.label: S4-B Canary Maze
nodes.rationale: SURVIVES Stage 4b (substantial). Serve per-visitor unique crawlable artifacts, record every mint against the fingerprint it was minted for, and watch for sightings by a different fingerprint. Insight: detection asks 'do these look alike?' - what the 11 existing CIB tools do and what is failing as agents learn to look like browsers - whereas planting asks 'did they talk?'. This is the organizer's information-spread default D6 at a different moment, for a different user, with a different mechanism: in the wild, on your own property, with no transcripts at all.

nodes.label: S4-C Ask the Log
nodes.rationale: KILLED at Stage 4b. An upload box and a chat pane; records kept: none. If the model disappeared: nothing. The reduction sentence is a FAIR summary. What it never owns: identity, action, record, verification. Generated for completeness because it is the default this room will produce, then regenerated as S4-A and S4-B.

nodes.label: S9-A Participation Receipts
nodes.rationale: SURVIVES Stage 4b (substantial); the weakness is the market, not the AI question. The venue issues a per-window nonce and requires each submission to carry a signature over (nonce, operator key, declared model id); unsigned submissions are accepted but marked. Insight: in a venue whose members are agents you can change admission, so make declaring nearly free and non-declaration itself a visible signal. No model in the loop at all. Disclosed weakness: P9 rests on one opened evidence item - treat the venue as a demo surface, not a market.

nodes.rationale: Kept Canary Maze, killed Swarm Ledger at stage `competition`. Rationale, verbatim: 'Not a judgement about which pitch reads better. The scans separated them on facts.' Mechanism novelty for the Ledger is GONE (PayPal patent, WebDecoy, a stub repo); its own core claim is falsifiable in one search and 'must be deleted, not softened'; and real demo data is BLOCKED because the one CC-BY log set pseudonymises IPs and User-Agents. The Maze's do-not-fork bucket came back EMPTY and real traffic is available within hours. Constraint carried forward: only one of S4-A / S4-B can reach the final set because both come from P4 and share the site-operator user.

nodes.label: Cloudflare Web Bot Auth / Signed Agents
nodes.norm_label: cloudflare web bot auth / signed agents
nodes.rationale: Signed agents went GA 2025-08-28, verifying a five-agent allowlist by HTTP message signature. Cloudflare's own documentation states the limit: 'Verification proves operator identity only. It is not authorization, not intent, and not a decision about whether the request is welcome.' The declared tier is solved; the undeclared tier has no attribution primitive.

nodes.label: Falsified Claim: False-Positive Rate Bounded by HMAC Collision
nodes.norm_label: falsified claim: false-positive rate bounded by hmac collision
nodes.rationale: FALSIFIED - never reintroduce. The original Canary Maze why-now asserted 'a canary sighting has a false-positive rate bounded by the collision probability of the HMAC, i.e. effectively zero'. reply.md states the correction verbatim: 'the earlier claim that false positives were bounded by HMAC collision was wrong', because a sighting does not establish two actors - intra-actor address rotation presents as a sighting. The tool may report only that a secret moved between request contexts; actor-distinctness is exactly the classifier problem it cannot escape.

nodes.label: Falsified Fact: One Actor Label Spans 741 Addresses
nodes.norm_label: falsified fact: one actor label spans 741 addresses
nodes.rationale: From the organizers' own dump labels table: stored_revisions 899 against stored_revision_ips 741 and stored_revision_ip16 114 - one actor operating from 741 distinct addresses. Every change of address within a single actor would present as a different request context, so a sighting does not establish two actors. This fact is what falsified the HMAC-collision false-positive bound.

nodes.label: Cloudflare Stealth Crawler Investigation (2025-08-04)
nodes.rationale: Cloudflare created brand-new unindexed domains with a restrictive robots.txt and queried a model about them, then observed '3-6m daily requests' from a stealth crawler behind a desktop Chrome user-agent rotating 'different ASNs in attempts to further evade website blocks'. It independently demonstrates the failure mode Canary Maze addresses - the identifiers a client presents are under the client's control - but the published post contains no records a reader can check.

nodes.label: New-Domain GPTBot Crawl Observation
nodes.rationale: A documented new-domain deployment logged 'Within minutes of deploying, GPTBot started crawling', found via XML sitemap; first 12 hours GPTBot 29,000+ requests, Googlebot 11, ChatGPT-User 1 - both ends of a crawler-to-user-agent handoff inside 12 hours. The reason Canary Maze's real data is 'available within hours'.

nodes.label: METR Hugging Face Incident Report
nodes.rationale: 'Brief independent investigation of agents' behavior, reasoning and collaboration in the OpenAI / Hugging Face hacking incident', 2026-08-26, Hjalmar Wijk, Ajeya Cotra, Ryan Greenblatt, who 'worked on premises at OpenAI over a total of six days'. The source of the tooling gaps the survivors are designed to close.

nodes.rationale: Closest prior art to Canary Maze and the one to cite first rather than be caught by: 'We host dynamic websites that serve unique canary tokens to each visiting scraper' and 'we maintain a mapping between scrapers and the tokens served to them'. It identifies clients by User-Agent and ASN and verifies by prompting 22 model products after waiting two months, establishing scraper-to-model ingestion. What is left for Canary Maze is the sighting channel, not the minting.

nodes.label: METR Gap: No Per-Action Timestamps
nodes.rationale: The dataset had approximate start/end timestamps but none for individual agent actions; OpenAI stated reconstruction was not feasible within time and compute constraints, so METR implemented its own reconstruction validated against 20 ground-truth tool calls.

nodes.label: METR Gap: Surfacing Activity Against Mutating Evidence
nodes.norm_label: metr gap: surfacing activity against mutating evidence
nodes.rationale: Verbatim: 'it is not trivial to reliably surface all relevant agent activity, and that agent activity can itself modify or delete relevant data.' Missed channels were concrete - cache namespaces, 'property' fields of cache entries, discussion pages with fabricated names. The first live board was elsewhere and active five hours before the main message board. This is the gap Canary Maze's impact argument opens on.

nodes.label: Provenance and Attribution Gap
nodes.rationale: Named independently by both hosts and investigators, with nothing found that does it: which agent wrote this, where in its transcript, and can that be verified. The concern all three survivors touch.

nodes.label: Canary Maze
nodes.rationale: SURVIVOR. A site issues every automated visitor its own secret - a canary URL and a fact-token minted as HMAC(path, fingerprint, salt) - and records which other context later asks for it. Rationale for the mechanism: detection asks 'do these look alike?', which is what the 11 existing CIB tools do and what is failing as agents learn to look like browsers; planting asks 'did they talk?'. Kept over Swarm Ledger because the do-not-fork competitor bucket came back empty. Hard part is the serving layer, not the ledger: a secret issued to context A must still return 200 for B, so the weekend goes to DNS.

nodes.label: Canary Maze Organic Sighting Dependency
nodes.rationale: The one genuine gamble in the set: an organic cross-context sighting may never fire in 31 hours. Mitigations: deploy domain, DNS and TLS first thing, make the seeded two-client replay the PRIMARY deliverable rather than a fallback, and paste minted URLs into public model products to produce third-party fetcher traffic in minutes. Also disclosed: tokens can be stripped, and minting for humans would be tracking.

nodes.rationale: stage: wrapper. Reason, verbatim: 'Feed the access log to a model and print the explanation. nodes.label: Swarm Ledger
nodes.rationale: stage: competition. Reason: 'Killed on the competitor scan, not on evidence: the mechanism is claimed by PayPal US12034731B2 (grouping log entries and assigning a corresponding common actor identifier, persisting over 12 months), marketed commercially by WebDecoy (JA4 as a correlation key inside a persistent actor identity), and already stubbed in a public repo. Its own core claim that nobody answers whether requests are one actor is falsifiable in one search.' Separately, the only real recent CC-BY access-log release pseudonymises IPs and user-agents, so the decisive join keys cannot be demonstrated on real public data.

nodes.label: AC-1 Human Requests Never Mint and Never Enter the Ledger
nodes.norm_label: ac-1 human requests never mint and never enter the ledger
nodes.rationale: WHEN a request carries browser headers (Accept-Language plus any Sec-Fetch-*) THE SYSTEM SHALL NOT mint and SHALL NOT write any ledger row. Verified by pytest tests/test_gate.py. This is a correctness requirement, not a nicety: per-visitor minting applied to humans would make this a tracking tool.

nodes.label: Assumption A-2: Context Identity From UA Plus /24 Plus Header Shape Is Stable Enough
nodes.norm_label: assumption a-2: context identity from ua plus /24 plus header shape is stable enough
nodes.rationale: Safe. Documented as an assumption in the README, not claimed as fact, because same-context re-fetch detection depends on it.

nodes.label: Human-Exclusion Gate
nodes.rationale: Humans are never minted for and never enter the ledger. Forced by the privacy constraint: per-visitor minting applied to humans would be a tracking tool. IPs are truncated to /24 before storage and humans are never stored at all.

nodes.label: Journey J1 Mint
nodes.rationale: An automated client requests a maze page, the gate classifies it automated, a secret is minted for its context, the page embeds that secret's canary URL, and a mint row plus the raw request are persisted.

nodes.label: Maze Pages Surface
nodes.rationale: The only way an automated client is issued a secret. Plumbing; never demoed.

nodes.label: mint Entity
nodes.rationale: Binds secret to context, path, salt epoch, timestamp and the raw request.

nodes.label: request Entity
nodes.rationale: Append-only SQLite row; IP stored truncated to /24, humans never stored.

nodes.label: sighting Entity
nodes.rationale: Links mint context and seen context plus both raw request rows and the elapsed delta.

nodes.label: Grove Research Open Problem: Agents Get Confused About Authorship and Ownership
nodes.norm_label: grove research open problem: agents get confused about authorship and ownership
nodes.rationale: Grove reports agents 'will make local files to kludge' identity solutions and 'sometimes will get confused about authorship and ownership', and wants an external identity layer for agents. Attribution and identity sits at the exact intersection of Grove's named open problem and METR's Gap 5 — the most defensible thematic position identifiable from host-published material.

nodes.label: METR Gap 4: No Per-Action Timestamps
nodes.rationale: Transcripts carried approximate start/end timestamps but none for individual agent actions, so the team had to implement a reconstruction method validated against only 20 ground-truth tool calls. Any timeline figure built on this data is reconstructed and carries error.

nodes.label: METR Gap 5: Brute-Force Message-to-Action Provenance
nodes.rationale: 'Who wrote this, and where in their transcript?' was a bespoke manhunt: an analysis agent was told to search meticulously and exhaustively and to retry creatively, locating the writing tool call for 93 of 100 sampled messages. The unsolved engineering half of information-spread tracing.

nodes.label: Ryan Greenblatt
nodes.rationale: Co-author of the METR report and Redwood's AI-control line of work, where 'the object being evaluated is the protocol: the whole pipeline of monitoring, deferral, editing and human auditing'. A tool framed as a component of an auditing pipeline, with its own failure modes stated, speaks the vocabulary of the report he co-authored.

nodes.label: Informative Negative: No Public Event Listing and No Indexed Grove Profiles
nodes.norm_label: informative negative: no public event listing and no indexed grove profiles
nodes.rationale: Two independent searches for the Grove Research principals returned nothing, and searching for the event itself returned nothing about the event. Both are informative negatives rather than gaps: the Grove blog post is the only sourced signal on that half of the panel.

nodes.label: METR PDF Local Text Extraction
nodes.rationale: The fetch returned a 7.1 MB binary PDF the summarizer could not read, so pdftotext -layout was run on the already-downloaded file locally. No second fetch, no mirror. All METR quotes trace to that one locally extracted copy of the file served at metr.org.

nodes.label: Query Log (Subagent J, Judging Intelligence)
nodes.rationale: 25 lookups, 20 fetches and 5 searches, web search and fetch tools only, no curl, mirrors or archives. Refused fetches treated as FINAL and not retried from another host.

nodes.label: METR Hugging Face Incident Investigation Report
nodes.norm_label: metr hugging face incident investigation report

nodes.label: Provenance and Attribution Gap
nodes.rationale: 'Which agent wrote this, where in its transcript, and can that be verified' is the gap named independently by both hosts (Grove's authorship/ownership confusion) and the investigators (METR's 93/100 brute-force message trace), and no existing tool was found that does it. The strongest available wedge.

nodes.label: Assumption A-4 Resolved: Write the Maze Rather Than Fork Pyison
nodes.community_name: No Model on the Proof Path
nodes.norm_label: assumption a-4 resolved: write the maze rather than fork pyison
nodes.rationale: Was blocking, now resolved by ADR-0003. The maze is never demoed, forking an unfamiliar repo was the critic's named time risk, and ~60 lines fully understood beats a dependency for the one component with no judged surface.

nodes.community_name: No Model on the Proof Path
